name: HSUS Farm Animal Protection Campaign: 2016 estimate (ACE)
summary: Campaigns for farmed animals in the US through corporate and public policy work, institutional meat reduction and social media. Animal Charity Evaluators' 2016 Guesstimate model: projected costs and achievements by program, converted here from ACE's years of suffering spared into suffering-adjusted days (SADs) per dollar, like our other animal models. ACE has since stopped publishing per-dollar estimates; this is the last public one for this charity.

sections.title: Model
sections.explainer:
Costs and accomplishments are projected by Animal Charity Evaluators for 2016 based on 2015 and the first six months of 2016. Read ACE's 2016 [review](https://animalcharityevaluators.org/research/charity-review/humane-society-of-the-united-states-farm-animal-protection-campaign/) of HSUS FAPC.

Because the Farm Animal Protection Campaign is just a part of the much larger Humane Society of the United States, it's especially difficult to understand their budget. The costs listed in the estimate reflect staff salaries, major grants restricted to HSUS FAPC that we know about, and some additional padding, but intentionally do not reflect other resources HSUS spends on farmed animal work through departments outside the FAPC. 

On the other hand, the achievements listed reflect the total achievements of HSUS related to farmed animals, regardless of the share of work done by the FAPC. It is impossible to fully separate the work done by FAPC from the work done by others at HSUS, and we think that FAPC plays a key role in leading other parts of the organization to address farmed animal issues.

This estimate, therefore, shows an overall picture of the FAPC using limited resources to catalyze changes that sometimes rely on the larger influence and resources of HSUS as a whole. We think this accurately reflects a reality in which the majority of FAPC's growth and funding come from **restricted** donations that fund the FAPC directly, but FAPC is able to use the credibility derived from being part of HSUS to influence both HSUS itself and other institutions. On the other hand, we note that **unrestricted** or even **not sufficiently restricted** donations to HSUS FAPC likely go to fund the rest of HSUS's work, and do not have the effects depicted here.

New institutional meat reduction policies
rows.explainer:
ACE's 90% interval, 60 to 100 (lognormal). The best guess is its median.

HSUS FAPC provided: "In 2015, HSUS garnered about 75 new institutional meat reduction policies in schools and hospitals across the country[.]"

rows.label: Average meals affected per institution per year
rows.explainer:
ACE's 90% interval, 200000 to 400000 (lognormal). The best guess is its median.

HSUS provided: "In 2015, HSUS garnered about 75 new institutional meat reduction policies in schools and hospitals across the country, resulting in over 20 million meat-containing meals being switched to meat-free meals."

This implies that HSUS estimates the average institutional policy affects 266,667 meals. We think this is a per-year estimate; it corresponds to about 5000 people eating 1 extra meatless meal per week for a year, which is a reasonable size for an average institution where school districts and universities are included. For comparison, several years ago HSUS helped convince the LA unified school district to adopt a Meatless Monday policy, and we estimate that that single policy change affected 34 million meals per year (but LAUSD is among the largest districts in the country, so the average institutional change is much less impactful than that one).

rows.label: Years of change accounted for
rows.explainer:
ACE's 90% interval, 1 to 15 (lognormal). The best guess is its median.

We account for a limited term of change, because organizations may revise their policies again or may have adopted the policy later without HSUS's influence. We think it is unlikely that most institutions would retain a policy for less than a full year, and we note that at least some institutions (e.g. LAUSD) have retained policies influenced by HSUS for four years now. HSUS only started working on institutional meat reduction five years ago, so this is a good sign that some policies can endure.

rows.label: Animals spared per meal
rows.explainer:
ACE's 90% interval, .0047 to .034 (lognormal). The best guess is its median.

We treat one meatless meal as equivalent to between 1/3 and 1/2 of a meatless day (depending on whether breakfast is counted as a meal at which one would normally eat meat, and because we think most of the meals we're accounting for are lunches and dinners). We use the estimate of the impact of a vegetarian year originally calculated for our [online ads report](https://animalcharityevaluators.org/research/interventions/online-ads/#V).

Corporate policy victories
rows.explainer:
ACE's 90% interval, 85 to 100 (lognormal). The best guess is its median.

HSUS FAPC's quarterly reports for Q1-Q3 2016 include mentions of around 80 corporate policy victories that they were involved in, mostly in Q1 and Q2. We think it's likely that the rest of the year will continue at a pace more similar to Q3, as there are few major companies left to approach about cage-free policies and no other type of campaign currently has the momentum that cage-free campaigns did earlier in 2016. Corporate policy victories tend to be slow to appear at first, then faster when companies perceive a new industry standard emerging.

rows.label: Animals affected by corporate policy victories
Hens affected yearly by cage-free policies HSUS FAPC was involved with
rows.explainer:
ACE's 90% interval, 80M to 130M (lognormal). The best guess is its median.

HSUS FAPC did not provide estimates for the number of animals affected by corporate policy changes they were involved with, so we have based our estimate on estimates from other groups active in promoting cage-free policies in the US.

rows.label: Proportional improvement in welfare due to cage-free policies
rows.explainer:
ACE's 90% interval, -.25 to .46 (normal). The best guess is its median.

Hens suffer in both battery cage and cage-free systems. While many advocates believe that cage-free systems are better from the hen's perspective, some disagree. Most research privileges outcomes of interest to farmers, rather than the hens' interests.

rows.label: HSUS FAPC's responsibility for changes
rows.explainer:
Beta(5, 5) in Guesstimate: best guess is its mean, range its 90% interval.

HSUS is often involved in corporate policy changes in cases where another group provokes a public image concern leading a corporation to seek help in writing a policy that will remove any pressure from them. While HSUS's role is less dramatic, we think they provide an essential resource even in this situation, and in some cases they are the only group involved in creating a change or are also involved in creating pressure to make the change, through advertising, investigations, or other means.

rows.label: Years of impact expected
rows.explainer:
ACE's 90% interval, 1 to 15 (lognormal). The best guess is its median.

We consider a limited term of impact because companies might simply have adopted the same policy later without HSUS FAPC's influence, might go out of business, or might abandon the policy after following it for some number of years.

rows.label: Equivalent hens spared from cage-free policies
Equivalent years of suffering spared from cage-free policies
rows.explainer: Since laying hens typically live for 1-2 years, the number of hens affected yearly is approximately the number of years of suffering reduced yearly (but we must correct for the fact that these hens are not spared from all the suffering involved in industrial agriculture). (A hen who lives for two years will be considered "affected yearly" for both of them, so does not need to be counted twice here.)

rows.label: Broiler chickens affected yearly by improved welfare policies HSUS FAPC was involved with
rows.explainer:
ACE's 90% interval, 200000000 to 1000000000 (normal). The best guess is its median.

HSUS FAPC did not provide estimates for the number of animals affected by corporate policy changes they were involved with, so we have based our estimate on estimates from other groups active in promoting broiler chicken welfare policies in the US. 

It's possible that some companies won't honor the policies they've agreed to. This is especially of concern in this case, since a single company is responsible for the majority of estimated impact to date.

rows.label: Proportional improvement in welfare due to improved policies
rows.explainer:
ACE's 90% interval, -.25 to .4 (normal). The best guess is its median.

Policies [include](http://www.npr.org/sections/thesalt/2016/06/27/483724603/in-quest-for-happier-chickens-perdue-shifts-how-birds-live-and-die) slaughtering chickens using gas instead of while fully conscious, adding windows and perches to barns, and potentially using slower-growth, higher-welfare breeds. The major risk is that the additional days of suffering due to slower growth could outweigh the welfare improvements due to the increased health of these birds.

rows.label: HSUS FAPC's responsibility for changes
rows.explainer:
Beta(6, 4) in Guesstimate: best guess is its mean, range its 90% interval.

While other groups have been involved in some policy changes to date, we would guess that HSUS is primarily responsible for corporate victories at this early stage, because of its wide public recognition.

Equivalent years of suffering spared from improved welfare policies
rows.explainer: Since broiler chickens usually live for 6-8 weeks, the equivalent number of years of suffering spared is around 7/52 the equivalent number of animals spared.

Monthly engaged users (Facebook)
rows.explainer:
ACE's 90% interval, 322000 to 436000 (lognormal). The best guess is its median.

HSUS FAPC's Facebook reports show an average of 379488 engaged users (anyone who clicks, comments on, shares, or reacts to the page) in a 28 day period. Estimated error due to variation over time is +/- 15%

rows.label: Yearly unique video views to 95% (Facebook)
rows.explainer:
ACE's 90% interval, 445000 to 602000 (lognormal). The best guess is its median.

HSUS FAPC's Facebook reports show 261663 unique views to 95% over 180 days. This leads to our mean estimate of 523326 unique views to 95% per year, with error due to changes over time of +/- 15%.
